evidence.label: Durrett PTE v5 (2019-01-11) printed p. 244: definition of uniform integrability for any collection; remark sup E|X_i| <= M+1

components.gap: C001: preserve Durrett's source variant of the definition (sec. 4.6, p. 244). The source defines uniform integrability for an arbitrary collection of random variables with no integrability hypothesis, and its remark that choosing M with the supremum below one gives sup_i E|X_i| <= M+1 < infinity makes integrability a consequence of the condition. The route's definition (body 15-35) is stated only for families of real integrable random variables, and nowhere on the route is it stated that the displayed condition itself forces integrability (the M+1 bound appears only in the annex proof for integrable families, annex 6-7). The hypothesis-free form, with integrability derived, is not supplied.

components.gap: C011: supply the whole cited extent 'thm. 4.6.9 and continuation' (Durrett pp. 247-248). After Levy's 0-1 law the source (a) quotes a line it attributes to Chung urging the reader to judge whether the result is obvious or incredible, (b) argues the 'obvious' reading (the best guess of 1_A given F_n should approach the best guess given F_infinity, which is 1_A), (c) argues the 'incredible' reading that yields Kolmogorov's 0-1 law, and (d) evaluates the result: the tail argument may not show it is 'too unusual or improbable to be possible', but it and later applications show it is very useful. The route supplies (c) (body 169-174; annex 293-303) and the mathematics behind (b) (annex 289-291), but not the attributed Chung line, the 'obvious' reading as a stated justification, or the source's evaluation (historical and evaluative claims omitted).

evidence.label: Durrett PTE v5 (2019-01-11) printed p. 248: Exercise 4.6.1 with its statistical reading, prior distribution and posterior distribution

components.gap: C016: supply Exercise 4.6.1's statistical reading and definitions (p. 248): with Z_i normal(0,1) the observations are a sample from a normal population with variance 1 and unknown mean; the distribution of theta is called the prior distribution; P(theta in . | Y_1,...,Y_n) is called the posterior distribution after n observations. The entry (body 256-270) uses 'integrable prior variable' and 'posterior consistency' but defines neither the prior nor the posterior distribution, does not state the normal-population reading, and does not connect E(theta | F_n) to the posterior. Hypotheses and the convergence proof are otherwise complete.
